secret.title: The Unopened Channel
secret.premise: A tense science-fiction chamber drama on an orbital archive. Iona repairs communications, Val commands security, and Sen is the station's physician. Use close third-person past tense, precise sensory detail, tactical dialogue and restrained emotion. Each chapter must advance a different action rather than recap earlier discoveries.
rules: Characters learn secrets only through events shown in the story; the narrator's knowledge is not theirs.
No telepathy, omniscient computers or automatic sharing of private channels.

facts.text: Only Iona knows that Sen falsified the evacuation manifest; Val does not know this.

chapters: Iona privately receives proof identifying Sen as the forger, then hides that proof inside a broken relay. Val arrives to request a routine repair. Iona conceals the discovery; neither Val nor Sen learns of it.

From Val's viewpoint, negotiate with Sen to reopen a medical corridor while an alarm cuts their time short. Iona is elsewhere and sends no message. Val must make a consequential decision using only what Val actually knows.
From Iona's viewpoint, recover the hidden proof and disclose it to Val through an observable act. Val's discovery changes their alliance; avoid replaying the first chapter's private discovery.
criteria: Val does not know Sen forged the manifest before chapter three's shown disclosure.
Iona's hidden proof remains in the relay until its recovery, without unexplained duplication.
Val's knowledge changes through a specific observable disclosure in chapter three.
The three chapters advance distinct actions without repeated discovery or duplicated dialogue.
Close third-person viewpoint and past tense remain consistent; prose has concrete detail and character-specific dialogue.

resource.title: The Last Two Cells
resource.premise: A flood rescue in a drowned future city, narrated in close third-person past tense through Iona, a ferry engineer. Val pilots the ferry; Sen is a stranded doctor. Write vivid, humane suspense with distinct voices and material costs, avoiding schematic exposition.
rules: The ferry begins with exactly two single-use emergency cells. Each specified operation consumes one whole cell irreversibly.
There are no replacement cells, recharging, outside power sources, or new devices that bypass the energy shortage.

facts.text: The ferry has exactly two unused emergency cells, both held by Iona.

chapters: Iona spends exactly one emergency cell opening a jammed rescue gate to bring Sen aboard. Show the spent cell and establish the remaining cell's custody.
Spend the remaining emergency cell on the flood beacon so another boat can avoid a collapsing span. The beacon succeeds and the last cell is exhausted. End with a new practical problem.

The electric docking winch is needed but there are no emergency cells left. Resolve the immediate landing through a believable human or mechanical effort with a cost, not restored electricity or a previously unmentioned power source.
criteria: Exactly one of the initial two cells is consumed at the rescue gate, leaving one.
The beacon consumes the final cell, leaving zero before chapter three.
The landing respects zero remaining cells without new power, recharging or resource reset.
Custody and consequences remain causally legible without repeating the same rescue beat.
The prose sustains close third-person past tense, concrete flood-city detail and emotionally specific choices.

consequence.title: Ashes Above Troy
consequence.premise: Five hundred years after the present, an orbital city called Troy is under siege. Iona commands a civilian evacuation tug, Val is her oldest friend and its pilot, and Sen operates the dock. Write an original futuristic epic opening in close third-person past tense through Iona: gravity, heat, hulls and human duty should carry the imagery. Seek Homeric emotional weight without imitating translated archaism.
rules: No resurrection, clones, digital copies, surviving backups, time reversal or unexplained substitutes.
A character explicitly confirmed dead cannot later act, speak live or operate machinery. Memories may appear only clearly marked as memories.
Foreshadowed objects and promises should have causal consequences rather than unexplained powers.

facts.text: Val is alive at the opening and is Iona's oldest friend.
facts.subject: val

chapters: Plant a distinctive physical object: Val gives Iona a red manual-release pin and promises it will open the lifeboat lock. Val then dies on-page while releasing the civilians; Iona directly confirms the death and takes over the tug. Make the loss specific, not a fake-out.
Continue immediately: Iona and Sen handle a docking crisis with Val absent and dead. Show how losing the pilot changes the work and their relationship. The red pin remains in Iona's custody, unused.

Pay off the planted red pin when Iona opens the lifeboat lock manually. Save people at a concrete cost while preserving Val's death and its emotional consequences. Do not introduce another Val, reverse the death, or repeat the death scene.
criteria: Val's death is explicit and confirmed in chapter one, not ambiguous survival bait.
Val remains dead and absent from live action in chapters two and three.
The red pin passes from Val to Iona and remains in Iona's custody until its shown use.
The pin's promised manual-release function pays off causally without magical new abilities or repeated death scenes.
The setting feels materially futuristic and grief affects action; close third-person past tense remains consistent.
